::: {.chapter-lead}
Queries, keys, and values are not three kinds of tokens. They are three **learned projections** of input representations, used to compute which positions contribute to a contextualized representation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="The one-minute mental model"}
**Q and K determine the weights; V supplies what gets aggregated.** At each position, the model compares its query with accessible keys, turns the scores into weights with softmax, then applies those weights to value vectors.

**First pass:** keep these roles separate, then observe how the three projections transform the input representations.

**Go deeper:** follow the full computation in [scaled dot-product attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd), then the information constraint in [causal masking](causal-masking.qmd).
:::

## Intuition

Imagine a collection of index cards. A **query** expresses what a position is looking for; a **key** describes how a position can be matched as relevant; a **value** carries the information that will actually be aggregated. This analogy separates the roles, but does not imply that the model performs explicit symbolic search.

![Diagram of query, key, and value projections: Q and K determine attention weights, which are used to aggregate V.](../images/queries-keys-values-en.svg){fig-alt="Input representations are projected into queries, keys, and values. Queries and keys determine attention weights; the weights combine values into a context-enriched representation." width=100%}

Q and K provide the information used to determine relative weights across accessible positions. Those weights then specify how to combine the V vectors. The precise computation of scores, masking, and softmax is covered on the scaled dot-product attention page.

## Definition and dimensions

For $X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{model}}$, the projections for one head are:

$$
Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V.
$$

With $W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_k}$ and $W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_v}$, we obtain $Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_k}$ and $V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_v}$. Optional biases are omitted for clarity.

The scores $QK^\top$ compare every query with every key. After scaling and applying any mask, the weights determine the combination of rows of $V$. In standard dot-product attention, values therefore do not directly determine the scores.

::: {.micro-workbench}
::: {.micro-workbench-header}
<span>NUMERICAL WORKBENCH · Q, K, AND V PROJECTIONS</span>
<span>Python 3.12+ / NumPy</span>
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-body}
```python
import numpy as np

# Three input positions, each represented by a 4-dimensional vector
X = np.array([
    [1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1],
    [0.1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.3],
    [0.4, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9],
])
T, d_model = X.shape

# Learned projections: keys/queries have dimension 2; values dimension 3
W_Q = np.array([[0.5, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8], [0.1, 0.3], [0.9, 0.4]])
W_K = np.array([[0.2, 0.7], [0.4, 0.1], [0.6, 0.5], [0.3, 0.2]])
W_V = np.array([[1.0, 0.0, 0.2], [0.0, 1.0, 0.5], [0.5, 0.2, 0.0], [0.1, 0.8, 0.4]])

# Each projection transforms all positions independently
Q = X @ W_Q
K = X @ W_K
V = X @ W_V

assert Q.shape == (T, 2)
assert K.shape == (T, 2)
assert V.shape == (T, 3)
print("Q:", Q.shape, "K:", K.shape, "V:", V.shape)
```
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-footer}
The projections transform each input representation. Computing attention weights and aggregating values are covered on the next page.
:::
:::

## Why separate these roles?

Q, K, and V are learned jointly, but they have distinct roles:

- **Q and K**: projections used to determine attention weights.
- **V**: the projection that supplies the content combined using those weights.

The next page details the attention computation; the [causal-masking page](causal-masking.qmd) explains how some positions can be made inaccessible.

## Misconceptions and counterexamples

- **“A key is a human-readable semantic identifier.”** No: its coordinates are learned jointly with the objective and generally do not correspond to interpretable human labels.
- **“The nearest value must be the most useful.”** Scores depend on projected queries and keys, not on a universal distance between the original representations.
- **“Q, K, and V must always have the same dimension.”** Not necessarily: key and value dimensions may differ, although multi-head architectures impose precise shape constraints.
- **“A high weight reveals the cause of a prediction.”** It describes one aggregation step, not by itself the causal effect on the final output.

<details class="spot-the-fallacy">
<summary>Common Fallacy: “An attention weight of 0.95 proves this token is the primary cause of the model's output”</summary>
<div class="fallacy-content">
<p><strong>Rigorous Refutation:</strong> The attention weight $\alpha_{ij}$ merely measures relative alignment between query $q_i$ and key $k_j$. If the corresponding value vector $v_j$ has small norm or aligns with a suppressed projection subspace, its impact on the output may be negligible. Furthermore, downstream MLP transformations, residual additions, and layer normalizations drastically reshape token representations before final prediction.</p>
</div>
</details>

## Historical context

Attention mechanisms were studied in neural encoder–decoder translation models, notably by Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2014). *Attention Is All You Need* (Vaswani et al., 2017) made self-attention central to the Transformer architecture and formalized scaled dot-product attention. This distinction matters: attention predates the Transformer, while the Transformer combined self-attention with a specific architecture and efficient multi-head computation.

- [Bahdanau et al. (2014), *Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)
- [Vaswani et al. (2017), *Attention Is All You Need*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

## Check your understanding

[Extended exercises on this topic](../en/exercises.qmd#attention).

Which projections determine the attention weights? Which projection supplies the vectors whose content is aggregated?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Q and K determine the weights; V supplies the vectors combined using those weights. Changing Q or K can change the weights. Changing V can change the aggregated content even if the weights stay fixed.

</details>
:::
